description: A small coin buys admission to an early movie setting.
cardDescription: A small coin buys admission to an early movie setting.
focus: The setting is a Nickelodeon Ticket Window. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Motion picture shown on a screen
Place for one person to sit
Keyboard instrument used to accompany silent films
Describing a film made without synchronized spoken dialogue
Image made with a camera or pencil
Entrance area outside a concert auditorium
Spool storing film or fishing line
Fabric panel hung at a window

answerNotes.NICKEL: A U.S. nickel is worth five cents. The name does not mean the entire coin is made of pure nickel.
answerNotes.TICKET: A ticket can give admission or identify an item left for a service. A theater ticket and a dry-cleaning claim ticket serve different uses.
answerNotes.WINDOW: A window admits light through glass. A screen is a mesh barrier that can keep insects out when the glass is open.
answerNotes.FILM: Film can mean the strip used to record pictures or the finished movie. A projector moves the strip to display successive images.
answerNotes.SCREEN: Screen can mean a display surface or a mesh barrier. The phone and movie scenes use the display meaning; a porch door uses the mesh meaning.
answerNotes.PIANO: A piano sounds when keys cause hammers to strike strings. In silent-film theaters, a live pianist sometimes supplied the accompaniment.
answerNotes.COIN: A coin is a metal piece of money. The value depends on the currency and period; Bible stories do not use modern U.S. coins.
answerNotes.REEL: A reel stores a long flexible strip or line. A fishing reel takes up line, while a film reel holds a strip of images.

solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Common name for a U.S. one-cent coin
Chewy candy often colored black or red
Brown sweet made from cocoa beans
Raised surface where customers are served

answerNotes.JAR: A jar has a wide opening that makes spooning and filling easier. A bottle usually has a narrower neck.
answerNotes.SWEET: Sweet describes flavor, not temperature or texture. A food can be sweet and cold, or sweet and warm.
answerNotes.BAG: A bag is a flexible carrying container. A pocket is generally a smaller compartment attached to clothing or another bag.
answerNotes.COUNTER: A counter is a raised work or serving surface. In a shop it separates the customer area from the worker's space.
answerNotes.GLASS: Glass is usually transparent but can also be colored. A glass is a drinking vessel, while glass without an article can name the material.

title: A Telephone Booth on the Corner
subtheme: A Telephone Booth on the Corner
description: A public telephone waits inside a small glass-sided booth.
cardDescription: A public telephone waits inside a small glass-sided booth.
focus: The setting is a Telephone Booth on the Corner. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Small enclosed space containing a public telephone
Everyday short name for a telephone
Money piece such as a nickel
Telephone term traditionally used for the part held to the ear
Movable panel at a room's entrance
Say a name to get attention
Person who once helped connect telephone calls

answerNotes.PHONE: Phone is the everyday short form of telephone. Older sets had dials and receivers; newer ones can also show video.
answerNotes.COIN: A coin is a metal piece of money. The value depends on the currency and period; Bible stories do not use modern U.S. coins.
answerNotes.DIAL: A dial can show numbers on a clock, telephone, or radio. Its marks identify times, phone choices, or station frequencies according to the object.
answerNotes.RECEIVER: An older telephone receiver combined the parts for hearing and speaking. Returning it to its cradle ended the call.
answerNotes.CORD: A cord can carry electricity or connect equipment. In an older telephone, the coiled cord let the handset move away from the base.
answerNotes.GLASS: Glass is usually transparent but can also be colored. A glass is a drinking vessel, while glass without an article can name the material.
answerNotes.DOOR: A door is the movable panel at an entrance. Hinges let it swing, while a latch or lock holds it closed.
answerNotes.CALL: Call can mean telephone contact or saying a name aloud. Both uses involve trying to get someone's attention.
answerNotes.NUMBER: A number can count an amount or identify something. A telephone number identifies a connection rather than measuring its size.
answerNotes.NICKEL: A U.S. nickel is worth five cents. The name does not mean the entire coin is made of pure nickel.
answerNotes.DIME: A U.S. dime is worth ten cents. Two nickels have the same value, although they are different coins.

Short everyday name for a bicycle
Flexible sack with an opening at the top
Covered area at a house entrance
Bring something to its intended address
Material used for writing or wrapping
Prominent title above a newspaper story

answerNotes.ROUTE: A route is a planned course. Several roads or stops can be parts of a single route.
answerNotes.BAG: A bag is a flexible carrying container. A pocket is generally a smaller compartment attached to clothing or another bag.
answerNotes.PORCH: A porch is an outdoor entrance area, often with a roof. A patio is usually a paved sitting area at ground level.
answerNotes.STEP: Step can name an action or one level of a stairway. In a stepping-stone clue, it concerns placing a foot on the next surface.
answerNotes.DOOR: A door is the movable panel at an entrance. Hinges let it swing, while a latch or lock holds it closed.
answerNotes.PAPER: Paper can be folded, cut, and written on. Card stock is heavier and stiffer, making it useful for tags and greeting cards.
answerNotes.FOLD: Folding brings one part of a sheet over another. A crease is the line left by pressing that fold.
answerNotes.STREET: A street is a road through a built-up area. Its name and building numbers form part of a postal address.
answerNotes.HOME: Home can mean a dwelling or the local side in a sporting match. Read the clue before applying the familiar household meaning.

words: Person whose trade includes cutting hair and shaving beards
Color of a clear daytime sky
Toothed grooming tool drawn through hair
Reflective surface used to form an image
Small fastener that grips papers together

answerNotes.POLE: A barber pole's stripes traditionally identify the shop. The moving pattern can make the stripes appear to travel upward or downward.
answerNotes.WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
answerNotes.CHAIR: A chair is intended for one sitter. A bench or sofa generally provides room for more than one person.
answerNotes.COMB: A comb has a row of teeth used to arrange hair. A brush uses bristles rather than a single row of rigid teeth.
answerNotes.BRUSH: A brush holds many bristles in one handle. Their width and stiffness affect the marks or cleaning action it makes.
answerNotes.MIRROR: A mirror reflects light to form an image. Cleaning the surface removes marks; it does not change the reflected object.
answerNotes.SPIN: Spin means rotate around a center. A top stays upright while turning quickly, then wobbles as it slows.
